summary: A Murray County tower named Cohutta in one list sits about 9 km from the register's Cohutta Mountain frame, so the identity is unresolved.

facts.status_note: The cab is gone; the register says the metal frame remains.

events.note: Murray Fire Tower registered with the National Historic Lookout Register; the register places it on Cohutta Mountain.

evidence.supports: Murray entry: Murray County, 2,767 ft, coordinates
Register: tower on top of Cohutta Mountain in Fort Mountain State Park; metal frame remains, cab missing
evidence.quote: At Fort Mountain State Park, on top of Cohutta Mountain, the metal frame of the tower remains but the cab is missing.

evidence.supports: Register coordinates match the list's Murray entry
Register calls it the lost second tower of Fort Mountain
evidence.quote: lost second tower of Fort Mountain

evidence.supports: Register names the Georgia Department of Natural Resources as administering agency
Eastern list has a Cohutta Mountain entry
That entry is in Murray County, Fort Mountain State Park
evidence.quote: Murray County - Fort Mountain State Park

evidence.supports: Stone fire tower built by the CCC marks the summit of Fort Mountain
evidence.quote: A stone fire tower, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps and located in the park, marks the summit of the mountain.

evidence.supports: Park has a mountain lake, cabins, camping and public facilities
evidence.quote: The park also has a mountain lake, cabins, camping, and public facilities.

evidence.supports: CCC men arrived to build cabins, roads, a dam, two fire towers and a lake
evidence.quote: First 150 young men arrived at the Holly Creek Camp of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) to build cabins in which to live, then to build roads, a dam, two fire towers, and a lake in Fort Mountain State Park.

evidence.supports: The timeline entry for the CCC arrival is under 1933
Stone tower let rangers spot fires up to 40 miles away
evidence.quote: allowing rangers to spot fires up to 40 miles away so they could alert forest firefighters
A devastating blow to the historic tower occurred in 1971 when the upper wooden portion of the tower burned.

evidence.supports: Disrepair until 2014, when the state restoration began
evidence.quote: It stood in disrepair until 2014, when the Georgia Department of Natural Resources and its Parks, Recreation and Historic Sites division began the restoration process.

evidence.supports: Reopened after a $189,000 restoration, about a decade before the article
evidence.quote: A decade ago, 80 years after its completion, it also became a tangible reflection of a commitment to preserving history when the tower was reopened after its $189,000 restoration.

corrections.why: The register places the Murray Fire Tower on Cohutta Mountain at these coordinates, about 9 km west-southwest of the record's point. Confirm that the record means this tower before applying.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The list's Murray entry matches the register's coordinates to within about 0.0002 degree, so those two sources agree on one tower. The Cohutta point is the value they do not explain.

notes_for_editor: Identity unresolved. The record's point (34.78519, -84.62687) is about 8.9 km west-southwest of the register's Murray Fire Tower (34.750846, -84.714896), a distance calculated from the coordinates. The list's own Murray entry matches the register, so the record's point is either a different spot or a misplaced record. The story follows the register. The location correction is proposed only and needs a human decision. The stone CCC tower on Fort Mountain (list entry 'fort mtn', 34.78307, -84.70905) is a separate structure and may deserve its own record; the story mentions it for context only. Status now restates the register's wording (frame remains, cab missing). The earlier 'ruins' label was the editor's own, not from any source, and has been removed. The register does not say whether the frame can be climbed, and the park is public. The brief's 'EE1864' datasheet tag could not be checked against any source.
